reader.summary: During the reporting window, Indonesia was struck by two simultaneous crises. First, devastating wildfires—described as the worst in over a decade—killed four firefighters at Mount Bromo national park and produced a thick orange-toxic haze that blanketed the country and spread across Southeast Asia. The haze closed schools in East Timor, drove Singapore's pollution to record levels, and prompted Singapore to name seven Indonesian firms as responsible. Indonesia's president offered to accept foreign assistance, and the country doused its skies with dry ice in a desperate bid to clear the air. Second, MSCI launched a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia from emerging-market to standalone-market status, triggering the worst single-day stock decline since 1998. The government unveiled 117 million dollars in trading fines, analysts warned of capital outflows, and the rupiah came under pressure. Meanwhile, a fuel crisis forced days-long lines at Bali gas stations, the electricity chief was replaced after a major Batam blackout, Indonesia's top Islamic council opposed upcoming Andrea Bocelli concerts over Israel ties, and women's professional football restarted after a seven-year absence.

display.eli5:
Indonesia is going through a really rough stretch. Big fires are burning in the forests and the smoke is so thick that the sky turns orange and people struggle to breathe outside. Some firefighters died trying to put out the fires at a volcano park, and the haze has spread so far that schools in Timor had to close and Singapore's air quality hit record pollution levels.

At the same time, a big international ratings company called MSCI is thinking about removing Indonesia from its list of major investment markets. This scared off a lot of investors, and the stock market had its worst single-day drop since 1998. The rupiah, which is Indonesia's money, is getting weaker and weaker.

Next week, the fires will probably get worse before they get better, and the government will call in help from neighboring countries. The stock market will stay jumpy, and the central bank will probably raise interest rates to try to protect the currency. The gas shortage in Bali should start to get better as more fuel trucks and tankers arrive.

What would be a real surprise? If people get so frustrated by the fires AND the money problems AND the gas lines all at once that they march in the streets of Jakarta, that would be a big deal. It would show the government is really losing the patience of the people.
